subtype_info: Pott's disease with bilateral psoas abscess
title: Mistaken identity: Reporting two cases of rare forms of extrapulmonary tuberculosis in Solomon Islands
case_text:
A 34-year-old Melanesian female presented to the emergency department with normal vital signs, flank pain, and low-grade fever. The patient had a history of a Bartholin abscess, right ovarian cyst, and self-resolved pleural effusion within the past year but no history of TB infection. The patient was treated outpatient for a suspected UTI within the past year with a standard regimen of nitrofurantoin (100 mg 2x/day), metronidazole (400 mg 3x/day), with acetaminophen, and ibuprofen for pain management. Nevertheless, back pain persisted for 7 months. On re-admission, the patient was referred to gynecology and was again treated outpatient for a suspected UTI with trimethoprim (300 mg 1x/day) and acetaminophen for pain. When the patient returned 10 days later with persistent bilateral flank pain, her medical team adjusted her treatment regimen to amoxycillin (500 mg 3x/day), metronidazole (400 mg 3x/day), nitrofurantoin (100 mg 2x/day) and acetaminophen. Additionally, an ultrasound of the abdomen and kidneys was ordered, and the patient was referred to the surgical team.
When the patient presented to the surgical ward to review her ultrasound results, her flank pain had spread to include the upper lumbar region (L1 & L2). Ultrasound revealed complex collection (10.5 x 4.8 x 7.4 cm) inferior to the right kidney with loss of the normal proximal aspect of the right psoas muscle. A follow-up CT of the abdomen pelvis was scheduled, and the patient was placed on a regimen of cloxacillin (500 mg 4x/day), ibuprofen, and acetaminophen. The patient independently sought out kastom medicine, a traditional set of herbal and spiritual medical practices in Solomon Islands, before returning for her CT two months later.
Radiologic imaging (Fig. 1) revealed bony destruction of the T8-T12 vertebrae with a loss of height and kyphosis of T11. Of further concern, bone and inflammatory debris of T11 was noted to be encroaching into the spinal canal at the T11-T12 level. Lytic lesions were also visualized on the L1 and L2 vertebrae. A paravertebral abscess was seen extending from T8 to L1 and a bilateral psoas abscess was visualized. The psoas abscess was irregular in distribution, measuring 5 x 4.3 x 15.3 cm on the right side and 1.1 x 1.3 x 3.4 cm on the left. Additionally, focal omental lymphadenopathy was seen in the right lower quadrant. The limited view of the lungs (below T6) showed septal thickening and consolidation in the right middle lobe. A functional right ovarian cyst (3.3 x 2.8 cm) was also noted.
A surgical registrar performed an incision and drainage (I&D) of the psoas abscess with tubes inserted bilaterally for continuous drainage. A total of 10 mL of straw-colored fluid were drained from the right side with minimal collection (<2 mL) drained from the left abscess over two days. The surgical team collected a sample of fluid from the right psoas abscess for laboratory analysis. When this sample did not culture, the surgical team suspected TB and screened the patient for TB exposure. Further questioning revealed that the patient had been the primary caretaker for her mother during an infection of pulmonary tuberculosis four years prior. Subsequent mycobacterial testing was positive, and the patient was diagnosed with Pott's disease involving a bilateral psoas abscess. Importantly, chest x-ray was unremarkable in this case. The patient was discharged and placed on a nine-month treatment of HRZE1 with pyridoxine. On six-week follow-up the patient reported moderate resolution of flank pain and was observed to have permanent kyphosis. The patient acknowledged occasionally forgetting to take her medication.

Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: Pott's disease with bilateral psoas abscess
